summary: SCOUT SPHEREx is a public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx near-infrared data into short sky "movies," so anyone can spot objects that move or change brightness. Users enter a Right Ascension and Declination, in decimal or sexagesimal format, or pick one of the challenge's official targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. The backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for every SPHEREx image covering that spot. It converts the FITS cutouts into aligned, north-up PNG frames with one shared brightness scale, and the browser plays them in time order. Fast-moving stars are propagated by proper motion to the SPHEREx epoch, so they stay inside the cutout. A one-click comparison with unWISE epochs (2010–2023) makes decade-scale motion obvious. Every view lives in the URL, so it can be shared, bookmarked, or embedded in another website with an iframe. A bilingual (English/Spanish) guided tour and a learning catalog teach non-experts what to look for. Searching the sky has long been possible for volunteers; SCOUT SPHEREx makes it possible with SPHEREx's new data.
details:
What it does

SCOUT SPHEREx lets anyone explore how the sky changes over time using NASA's SPHEREx mission:

1. Pick a patch of sky. Type RA/Dec (133.7951, -7.2451 or 08h55m10.831s, -7d14m42.53s), or click one of the five official challenge targets. The view opens in an interactive Aladin Lite atlas.

2. Watch it as a movie. The tool finds every SPHEREx image of that position and plays the cutouts in chronological order. Controls include play/pause, step, a timeline slider, speed, and a detector selector (D1–D6). Each frame shows its date (UTC and MJD), detector and observation ID.

3. Compare across a decade. A second mode blinks unWISE epochs (NEO2→NEO11, ~2010–2023) at the same position, so high-proper-motion objects visibly slide across the field. PanSTARRS optical bands are also available.

4. Share and embed. Position, field of view and target are kept in the URL (/mision?ra=…&dec=…&fov=… or /mision?target=wise0855). Reloading, back/forward and copied links restore the same view. An embed=1 mode gives a compact view for iframes on other websites.

5. Learn first. A guided onboarding tour and a learning catalog (emission nebula, planetary nebula, spiral galaxy, Jupiter) show non-experts what each object looks like. Each catalog entry includes a recognition checklist, common pitfalls, and a link that opens the explorer centered on a real example. Jupiter's link uses its position computed for the current date.

How it works

- Backend (Python / FastAPI):

- Runs Simple Image Access (SIA v2) queries on the IRSA spherex_dr1 collection with astroquery/pyvo.

- Downloads the FITS cutouts in parallel, reads the calibrated IMAGE extension and its celestial WCS, and reprojects every frame onto a common north-up TAN grid with reproject.

- Applies one shared ZScale + Asinh stretch (Astropy) so static sources don't jump in position or brightness, and serves the frames as PNG through a disk cache.

- Propagates proper motion with Astropy (apply_space_motion). Barnard's Star moves ~4.5′ between J2000 and the SPHEREx epoch, enough to fall outside a small cutout.

- Cutout URLs are restricted to IRSA (SSRF protection), and there is an offline fallback when IRSA is unavailable.

- Frontend (Vue 3 + TypeScript + Vite): Aladin Lite v3 for the sky atlas (DSS / 2MASS HiPS), Three.js for the 3D visuals, astronomy-engine for Jupiter's ephemeris, and English/Spanish i18n.

- Updating with new releases: the SPHEREx collection is a parameter, so new data releases (e.g., deep fields or DR2) can be used without code changes.

Benefits and impact

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, which is far more data than any team can inspect. Citizen-science projects like Backyard Worlds have shown that volunteers comparing images over time find brown dwarfs, comets and asteroids. SCOUT SPHEREx brings that workflow to SPHEREx data: it needs no installation and no astronomy background, and every view is a shareable link.

Creativity and design considerations

- A shared brightness scale and common reprojection make frames truly comparable, which matters for spotting real motion or variability.

- Proper-motion-aware targets, so fast movers are centered where SPHEREx actually saw them.

- Honest science: the interface explains that SPHEREx pixels are ~6″ and that its epochs are only months apart. That is why we pair it with WISE for decade-long motion, and why we note that brightness changes within one detector can come from wavelength differences across the filter.

- Accessibility and reach: bilingual interface, keyboard navigation, respect for reduced-motion preferences, and a responsive layout.

Tools used

Python, FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, reproject, NumPy, pandas, Pillow, pytest · TypeScript, Vue 3, Vite, Vue Router, Pinia, Aladin Lite, Three.js, astronomy-engine, Vitest · Git/GitHub.
